title: The thread of compassion
hook: make compassion the cotton, contentment the thread, restraint the knot and truth the twist (Asa di Var, ang 471)

segments.voice: Yesterday, sacrifice to the Guru, and your line: the turning point. Did you thank someone? Today, a turning point from Guru Nanak's own childhood, and the salok the tradition ties to it. Day five hundred fifty-four.

The courtyard is full. Relatives have come from nearby villages, food is cooking, and the family priest has arrived for an important day: a boy's investiture with the sacred thread. The boy is Nanak, still young, in Talwandi. The janamsakhis, the old life-stories of Guru Nanak written down generations later, tell what happened next. As the priest prepared the thread, the boy asked him a question. What is this thread for? Will it last? And then he described the thread he would actually wear, and it wasn't made of cotton at all.
screen: `A COURTYARD FULL OF RELATIVES.` → `THE BOY NANAK AND THE THREAD.` → `A THREAD NOT MADE OF COTTON.`

segments.voice: The janeu is a sacred thread that many Hindu families give their sons in a coming-of-age ceremony, worn across the body from the shoulder. For the families who keep it, it marks a second birth into learning and duty, and it's held with real reverence. The salok on ang 471, which Sikh tradition links to young Nanak's day, doesn't mock the thread. It asks for a deeper one. In paraphrase: make compassion the cotton, contentment the thread, restraint the knot, and truth the twist. This is the sacred thread of the soul. If you have it, priest, then put it on me. Daiaa, compassion, is the raw cotton, the stuff everything else is spun from. Santokh, contentment, which we met in the servants' pauri, is the thread itself, the long continuous strand. Jat, restraint, self-control, is the knot that holds it together. And sat, truth, is the twist that gives a thread its strength. Anyone who's ever spun yarn knows that untwisted fiber pulls apart in your hands. Truth is what makes the whole thing hold. Notice the order. Compassion comes first, as the material. Everything after that is shaping it. So a person could carry contentment and restraint and even truth, but without compassion there's nothing to spin. Sikhs remember this story as an early sign of who Nanak would become: not someone who rejects people's rituals for the sake of it, but someone always asking what's inside them. Tomorrow, we look at what he said such a thread could survive.
screen: `THE JANEU: A SACRED THREAD.` · `COMPASSION, THE COTTON.` · `CONTENTMENT, RESTRAINT, TRUTH.` · `TRUTH IS THE TWIST THAT HOLDS.` · then, large: `COMPASSION IS THE THREAD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: tie a thread and name the four. If you have a piece of string, yarn, or even a hair tie, hold it. If not, use your fingers. Touch it once and say, in your mind: compassion, the cotton. Run your fingers along it: contentment, the thread. Tie a loose knot: restraint, the knot. Give it a gentle twist: truth, the twist. Then hold it in your palm and breathe. If you pray, you can say Waheguru. The bell holds the time.
Janeu. The sacred thread. In Guru Nanak's salok, a thread of the soul: compassion the cotton, contentment the thread, restraint the knot, truth the twist.
Your line: compassion is the thread. Today, if you tied a string, keep it in your pocket. Each time you touch it, do one small kind thing. Day five hundred fifty-four.

screen: `DAY 554 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE THREAD THAT WON'T BREAK.`

howItsDone: Sikhs remember the janamsakhi story of young Nanak and the sacred thread, and hear this salok in the dawn singing of Asa di Var as a call to wear the inner thread of compassion.

fork.setup: you're the young Nanak, and the priest is ready to put the sacred thread on you. what do you do?
options: ask about a thread made of compassion, contentment, restraint and truth.
fork.reveal: the janamsakhis say he asked what the thread was for, and described the thread of the soul: if you have it, put it on me.

original.note: Gurmukhi: janeu, the sacred thread given in a Hindu coming-of-age ceremony.

trapdoor: what you thought: a story about refusing a ritual.
what it means: a boy asking what's inside a ritual, and naming a thread of compassion, contentment, restraint and truth.
what a scholar hears: daiaa kapaah, santokh soot, jat gandhee, sat vatt; the link to Nanak's childhood comes from the janamsakhis, not the salok itself.

sources.ref: Asa di Var, salok M1 (daiaa kapaah santokh soot), Ang 471

notes: The salok is paraphrased; confirm 'daiaa kapaah santokh soot jat gandhee sat vatt / eh janeoo jeea kaa hee ta paade ghat'.

The janeu ceremony (upanayana) is described respectfully and briefly; a Hindu reader should not feel mocked. Confirm wording 'many Hindu families... their sons' and 'a second birth into learning and duty'.

The janamsakhi episode (priest named Hardyal in some accounts; Nanak's age varies by account) is told as tradition with details kept general; confirm. The salok's link to the childhood episode is traditional, not stated in the text.
Spinning detail (twist gives yarn strength) is the narrator's illustration.
